tldr: The authors propose "TouchSight," a framework for predicting dense contact forces across the entire hand solely from standard egocentric RGB videos, without requiring specialized tactile gloves. By re-rendering gloved recordings into bare-hand videos using generative video AI, they bridged the appearance gap between gloved hands and bare hands while perfectly preserving the ground-truth measured force labels. This yielded "TwinTouch-20H," a 20-hour paired dataset that enables highly accurate force prediction.
hero_caption: The overall framework of TouchSight. It is trained jointly on 500 hours of HumanTouch data measured with pressure gloves, TwinTouch data converted to bare-hand videos via generative AI, and five HOI datasets with geometric contact labels. At inference time, TouchSight operates purely on monocular RGB videos without relying on tactile gloves or external hand pose estimators, accurately predicting per-taxel forces on both hands as well as hand contact states.
overview:
For robots to perform dexterous manipulation like humans, "tactile sensing"—knowing where and how much force is being applied—is essential. However, tactile sensing requires direct measurement at contact interfaces. Collecting data at scale has traditionally demanded expensive and fragile tactile gloves, making it difficult to scale up as visual datasets do. On the other hand, everyday egocentric videos contain rich implicit contact cues, but they lack ground-truth force labels due to the absence of physical sensors.

To solve this dilemma, the authors came up with an approach to re-render gloved video recordings into "bare hands" against "diverse backgrounds" using a generative video model (Seedance 2.0). Through this, they constructed "TwinTouch-20H," a 20-hour dataset paired with bare-hand RGB video while fully preserving the precise, measured force labels. Furthermore, they designed "TouchSight," an architecture that does not rely on external hand pose estimators, but instead integrates semantic and geometric features to decode forces via region queries.

Experiments confirmed that TouchSight significantly outperforms prior methods in native pressure glove force prediction, bare-hand transfer performance, and contact prediction on the OakInk2 benchmark. The authors also demonstrated that force prediction accuracy scales consistently with larger tactile datasets, opening up a pathway to annotate arbitrary egocentric videos with pseudo-tactile labels in the future.
contributions: Constructed "TwinTouch-20H," a 20-hour paired dataset that leverages a generative video model to convert gloved videos into bare-hand videos in new backgrounds while fully preserving ground-truth measured force labels.

Proposed the "TouchSight" architecture, which operates without external hand pose estimation or mesh reconstruction during inference by symmetrically fusing foundation model features (semantics and geometry) and decoding forces with region queries.

Established a mixed-supervision training framework capable of simultaneously learning from measured force data and geometric contact labels from existing HOI (hand-object interaction) datasets through shared region queries.
Demonstrated that force prediction accuracy scales consistently as tactile data supervision expands, showing strong zero-shot generalization to unseen, natural real-world egocentric videos.

sections.heading: Why try to estimate touch purely from sight?
sections.summary: Tactile sensing is essential for dexterous robot manipulation, but collecting large-scale data is extremely difficult because sensors must be worn. To break this bottleneck, the authors propose TouchSight, a new method that predicts dense, full-hand contact forces directly from everyday egocentric videos.
sections.details:
Vision can capture hand positions and movements, but it cannot directly observe the exact moment of contact, grip strength, or pressure distribution across the hand. While tactile feedback is crucial for dexterous manipulation, tactile gloves are very expensive and mechanically fragile, degrading rapidly under repetitive loads. As a result, gathering thousands of hours of data—as done in vision learning—has been physically constrained.

Meanwhile, vast amounts of human egocentric videos already exist, implicitly carrying rich contact information. If we could accurately recover full-hand tactile signals just by looking at video, those tactile signals could be utilized for downstream robot policy learning. However, prior research has been restricted to small-scale datasets of a few hours or limited to predicting binary contact presence derived from mesh-to-mesh proximity, falling short of estimating actual measured force magnitudes.

Moreover, existing methods suffer from an architectural weakness: they rely on external hand pose estimation tools (such as MANO reconstruction). During contact, severe occlusions and motion blur from hands and objects drastically degrade reconstruction accuracy. In this work, the authors build on 500 hours of measured tactile data from "HumanTouch," introduce "TwinTouch-20H" where gloved footage is converted to bare hands via generative video models, integrate existing geometric contact data, and propose TouchSight to predict forces directly from monocular RGB video without external hand reconstructors.

sections.heading: Prior work on tactile sensing and vision-based tactile prediction
sections.summary: Tactile data collection has evolved from flat tactile pads to sensorized gloves, yet scaling and appearance gaps have remained enduring challenges. This work sets itself apart through large-scale measured force data, generative AI-driven bare-hand domain adaptation, and a novel architecture free of external reconstructors.
sections.details:
### II-A Tactile Sensing for Dexterous Manipulation
Optical tactile sensors like GelSight and vision-tactile cross-modal models have driven success in insertion and in-hand regrasping policies. However, achieving stable grasps with multi-fingered hands requires coordinated contact adjustments across the entire palm, not just the fingertips. The cost of collecting data covering the whole hand has been the greatest bottleneck. TouchSight drastically cuts this cost by predicting tactile feedback directly from video without needing sensors at capture time.

### II-B HOI Tactile Datasets
Existing tactile datasets have faced a trade-off between precision and scale. Studies using flat sensors are confined to planar interactions, while those using tactile gloves (such as EgoTouch) remain limited to a few hours or thousands of episodes. Although large-scale HOI datasets exist, their contact labels are binary, obtained from mesh proximity or thermal imaging, lacking actual force magnitudes. This work builds upon the largest measured force dataset (HumanTouch) while using a generative model to transform gloved appearances into bare hands, achieving both precise measured force labels and visual diversity.

### II-C Predicting Tactile Information from Vision
Early attempts estimated contact forces from hand and object dynamics or predicted pressure from planar hand images. Recently, methods have emerged to predict dense tactile maps onto MANO 3D mesh vertices or sensor grids. However, most prior methods require estimated 3D joint positions or external hand reconstructors as input during inference, leaving them brittle under contact-induced occlusions. TouchSight differs fundamentally by eliminating external reconstructors entirely and decoding forces directly from pixels using region queries.

sections.heading: Turning gloves into bare hands with generative AI: TwinTouch-20H
sections.summary: Recordings with tactile gloves look unnatural, and their backgrounds are often monotonous. Using generative video models, the authors re-rendered gloved hands into bare hands and replaced backgrounds with diverse everyday scenes, building a 20-hour paired video dataset with intact ground-truth force labels.
sections.details:
### III-A TwinTouch-20H Overview
The high-precision tactile glove data from "HumanTouch" (500 hours) is extremely valuable, but it was recorded in a fixed environment with a black background and a white table. Because the hands are covered by bulky sensor gloves, there is a severe domain gap with real-world bare-hand footage. To bridge this, the authors used a state-of-the-art video generation model, "Seedance 2.0," to re-render 10 hours of video uniformly sampled across 52 tasks in HumanTouch into bare-hand videos across 10 diverse backgrounds. This yielded "TwinTouch-20H," a 20-hour paired dataset consisting of 10 hours of original gloved videos and 10 hours of generated bare-hand videos.

### III-B Data Generation Pipeline and Quality Control
The generation pipeline uses prompts to replace sensor gloves with bare hands and transform the black background and white desk into new environments like living rooms and kitchens, complete with appropriate table textures and ambient props. Because hand movements and geometric relationships during object manipulation are preserved, the taxel-level measured force labels recorded by the gloves serve directly as ground truth for the bare-hand videos.

To prevent hand distortions and object disappearance common in generative AI, strict quality control was enforced. Specifically, the original gloved video was superimposed over the generated video at 40% opacity for visual verification. Any samples showing artifacts—such as non-erased gloves, unnatural hand warping, altered manipulated objects, or drifted trajectory paths—were discarded. Only high-quality data with perfect geometric alignment was retained.

captions.F2: Examples from TwinTouch-20H. Across 52 interaction tasks and 10 scenes, the original gloved videos (left) and the generative AI videos converted to bare hands with diverse backgrounds (right) share identical ground-truth measured tactile labels.

sections.heading: TouchSight architecture: No reliance on external hand pose estimators
sections.summary: TouchSight extracts semantic and geometric features from two frozen vision foundation models (DINOv3 and VGGT) and fuses them via bidirectional cross-attention. Through "region queries" assigned to hand and finger parts, it simultaneously decodes per-taxel contact forces and contact states on MANO meshes.
sections.details:
### IV-A Problem Formulation
The input is an egocentric RGB clip $\mathbf{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 3\times H\times W}$ of $T=8$ frames. The objective is to predict the tactile state of both hands in each frame. For glove data, the model predicts continuous force vectors over $V_{\mathrm{valid}}=275$ reliable taxels per hand. For general HOI data without force sensors, it predicts binary contact states $\hat{\mathbf{C}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 2\times 778}$ across the palmar surface among MANO's 778 vertices. At inference time, no external hand pose estimators or hand mesh reconstructors are used.

### IV-B Visual, Geometric, and Temporal Encoding
Recognizing contact requires not only visual appearance (semantics) but also 3D spatial distances (geometry). Therefore, two frozen foundation models are adopted: DINOv3 (ViT-B/16) for semantic feature extraction and VGGT for geometric reasoning. After projecting tokens from both models into a shared dimension $D=512$, a 2-layer bidirectional cross-attention block fuses information symmetrically. Furthermore, to capture temporal contact dynamics (approach, compression, release), "Divided Space-Time Attention" is applied to produce a spatio-temporal feature memory $\mathbf{M}$.

### IV-C Region-Query Force Decoder
Force application varies across anatomical parts of the hand. The authors define $Q=10$ "region queries" per hand (20 for both hands), comprising one query for each finger (5 total) and five partitioned band regions across the palm (5 total). These queries attend to the spatio-temporal memory $\mathbf{M}$ via cross-attention and are further refined along the time axis by a temporal encoder. The final force for each taxel is generated by FiLM-modulating (affine feature transformation) a learnable taxel embedding $\mathbf{e}_{h,v}$ with its corresponding region query $\mathbf{q}_{h,r}$. The same region queries are shared to determine contact on MANO vertices.

### IV-D Mixed Supervision and Loss Functions
Taxel-level continuous forces from glove data and binary contact labels (thresholded at hand-object distance under 1 cm) from five public HOI datasets (HOT3D, TACO, HOI4D, H2O, ARCTIC) are trained together in a mixed-supervision batch. Force regression combines Huber loss with an $L_1$ loss in a scale-normalized space that preserves zero contact, assigning a 10× weight to high-force taxels. Contact prediction employs a weighted binary cross-entropy loss over palmar vertices, trained end-to-end via a linear combination of both objectives.

captions.F4: Overall architecture of TouchSight. Features from frozen DINOv3 and VGGT are symmetrically fused, processed through spatio-temporal attention, and fed into 20 shared region queries. The queries branch into a force prediction head and a contact classification head, operating solely on monocular RGB during inference.

sections.heading: From measured force prediction to zero-shot generalization on unseen videos
sections.summary: Experiments validate the necessity of geometric features and temporal modeling for force prediction, showing that training on generative bare-hand data substantially improves accuracy. TouchSight achieves SOTA in contact prediction on OakInk2 and displays a clear scaling law where performance steadily improves with more tactile data.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
Training utilizes three data streams: HumanTouch (measured force), TwinTouch (generated bare-hand + measured force), and five HOI datasets (geometric contact). Evaluation metrics include Mean Absolute Error over all taxels (MAE), error over active taxels under force ($\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{act}}$), Volumetric IoU (Vol.IoU) assessing spatial force overlap, and temporal Pearson correlation (Temp.Pearson). Binary contact estimation is evaluated via AUROC, IoU, Precision, Recall, and F1.

### V-B Measured Force Prediction and Ablation
In native tactile glove space evaluations, removing VGGT (geometric features) degraded all metrics, especially temporal correlation, highlighting the importance of 3D geometric awareness in tactile prediction. Removing the temporal module caused a large drop in active taxel error and temporal correlation. Without temporal structure, the model safely predicts near-zero values for inactive taxels, failing to capture actual contact dynamics.

### V-C Bare-Hand Generalization and HOI Benchmarks
On bare-hand force prediction using the TwinTouch test set, adding generative AI data (AIGC) to training clearly improved all metrics. On the real-world OakInk2 benchmark for binary contact prediction, TouchSight outperformed prior methods BSTRO, DECO, and HACO, achieving the highest AUROC, IoU, Precision, and F1 (0.536). While HACO exhibited high Recall due to over-predicting contact, its Precision was very low; TouchSight captured much sharper and localized contacts. Furthermore, on completely unseen in-the-wild egocentric videos from Ego-Exo4D and Ego4D, TouchSight achieved visually plausible zero-shot predictions of contact force distributions during tasks like rotating tires or washing bowls.

### V-D Scaling Law of Tactile Data Volume
Scaling experiments varying the HumanTouch training data volume across 0%, 10%, 25%, 50%, and 100% revealed consistent reductions in active taxel error and improvements in temporal correlation as data scaled. The largest boost occurred when introducing the first 10%, followed by steady, predictable performance scaling as more data was added.

captions.F6: Force prediction results from bare-hand videos on TwinTouch test clips. While the input is bare-hand RGB only, the model accurately reproduces force-concentrated areas on both hands matching the paired glove ground truth (GT).
captions.F7: Qualitative comparison of binary contact prediction on OakInk2. Blue indicates vertices predicted as in contact. While prior methods like HACO over-predict contact across the entire hand, TouchSight (Ours) accurately captures sharp, localized contacts close to the ground truth (GT).
captions.F8: Zero-shot force prediction on unseen everyday egocentric videos (Ego-Exo4D, Ego4D, EgoDex). Even in uninstrumented outdoor videos, appropriate contact forces dynamically emerge across fingertips and palms during actions like turning a tire or washing a bowl.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Toward automatically generating tactile data from everyday videos
sections.summary: TouchSight predicts full-hand contact forces from egocentric video without external hand reconstructors, made possible by generative AI in TwinTouch-20H. Force accuracy scales with glove data volume, establishing TouchSight as a foundational technology to turn existing egocentric video corpora into tactile-annotated datasets.
sections.details:
This study presented TouchSight, a framework predicting dense full-hand contact forces solely from monocular egocentric videos. The primary obstacle—the domain gap between monotonous gloved training environments and diverse bare-hand real-world scenes—was successfully overcome by TwinTouch-20H, which re-rendered videos into bare hands using generative models while preserving measured labels.

Experimental results demonstrated that combining foundation models with region queries enables high-precision force prediction without relying on brittle hand pose estimators during inference. In addition, the authors confirmed that prediction performance steadily scales as tactile training data grows. This outcome suggests the feasibility of adding high-precision pseudo-tactile annotations to the vast amounts of human manipulation videos available online. Enabling models to learn not just "how hands move" but "how much force hands apply" directly from video holds great promise for accelerating dexterous robotic manipulation policies.

sections.heading: Appendix: Glove layout and region query correspondence
sections.summary: Details on the tactile glove sensor layout, valid taxel counts, alignment with MANO mesh vertices, and implementation details such as loss weights and data mixing ratios.
sections.details:
### A-A Glove Layout and Region Allocation
The tactile glove features a 23×20 grid (460 slots in total). Among them, 100 slots are padding and 85 are physically unreliable and excluded, leaving 275 valid taxels per hand (16 taxels × 5 fingers = 80, plus 195 on the palm). The 10 region queries oversee fixed spatial areas: each finger query covers 16 taxels, and the 5 palm queries cover 39 taxels each (195 / 5).

### A-B Supervision on Palmar MANO Vertices
Out of 778 vertices in the MANO mesh, 384 vertices belonging to the palmar surface are used for training and evaluation, excluding dorsal vertices. In glove data, 326 of these vertices correspond to measured taxel forces. In HOI data, all 384 vertices receive binary contact labels based on a nearest-object distance threshold of under 1 cm.

### A-C Training Hyperparameters and Data Mixing
The 54,931 episodes in HumanTouch are split into an 8:1:1 ratio. During batch sampling, HumanTouch receives the highest data mixing ratio, while the five HOI datasets are each assigned a 5% sampling weight. The force regression loss combines Smooth L1 (Huber) with $\beta=1$ and $0.5L_1$, applying a 10× loss weight to high-force taxels exceeding 5 glove units. The contact classification head loss is weighted by $\lambda_{\mathrm{cls}}=5$.

takeaways: Using generative video models (AIGC) to re-render visual appearances into bare hands and new backgrounds while retaining ground-truth sensor labels is a powerful data augmentation strategy to bridge sensor domain gaps.
Predicting the physical phenomenon of contact requires explicit modeling of 3D geometry (VGGT) and temporal transitions (Divided Space-Time Attention) alongside visual appearance (DINOv3).

Eliminating external hand pose estimation tools (like MANO fitting) from the inference pipeline and decoding forces directly from image features via region queries prevents failures during contact occlusions.
Force prediction accuracy scales consistently with larger tactile glove datasets, showing promising potential for building even larger tactile foundation models in the future.
limitations: Because video generative AI can occasionally cause object deformations or hand artifacts, human visual inspection using semi-transparent overlays is required for quality control, preventing full automation.

The predicted contact forces are constrained by the glove sensor layout (275 taxels on the palmar side only), meaning forces on finger sides, the back of the hand, or fingernails cannot be directly predicted.
Force prediction evaluations on unseen everyday videos remain limited to qualitative visualizations, leaving true physical force errors on unknown real-world objects unverified.
